title: Disagreeing well
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: qad in front of a PRESENT-shaped verb means may: qad yaʾtī ghadan, he may come tomorrow. It is the same particle L3-M7 taught in front of a past, where it means already, and the verb under it does not change.

English hedges with a modal — might, could, would — and every modal reshapes the verb behind it. Arabic has no modal at all: it hedges with a particle in front of an untouched verb, or with a whole frame.
The laysa paradigm, finished: lastu, lasta, lasti, laysa, laysat, lasnā, laysū. It negates a nominal sentence and never a verb, and the person sits inside the negation rather than beside it.

NEGATIVE RAISING, and for once the English transfer is safe: lā aẓunn anna hādhā ṣaḥīḥ is I don't think this is right. Both languages put the negative on the verb of thinking rather than inside the clause.
yabdū anna and min al-mumkin an are frames, not verbs to conjugate. They stay in the he-form whoever is speaking, and the person appears in the clause or the verb behind them.
ka- is a clitic meaning like, written joined the way L1-M2's bi- and L4-M2's fa- are. On L3-M3's annahu it makes ka-annahu, as if he.
ḥasanan, ʿalā ayy ḥāl and taqrīban are the softeners that let a refusal land as a pause. None of them is agreement; each buys a moment before the disagreement arrives.
Politeness here is not a verb form. This ladder has no conditional and writes no mood endings, so a soft no is built from particles and frames — never from a shape of the verb that English would use.

sentences.cue: I don't think this is right

words.note: L3-M3's aẓunn and aʿtaqid under a negative. The negative goes onto the thinking verb, exactly as it does in English — for once the transfer is safe.

sentences.trap: The logic is I think this is not right, and both languages move the negative forward onto the thinking verb. After four levels of interference this one really is a free ride.
sentences.sound: lā a-ẒUNN AN-na: the ẓ is the heavy dh, and the doubled nn of aẓunn is held.

variations.cue: I don't believe this is right
variations.changed: the verb of thinking: aẓunn → aʿtaqid, with nothing else moving

variations.cue: I don't think the manager is angry
variations.changed: the clause being doubted

mistake.why: It is grammatical and it is not what a speaker says. Arabic moves the negative forward as English does; leaving it inside the clause reads as a formal ruling.

sentences.usage: Disagreeing without contradicting — the softest no in the level.
sentences.mnemonic: Negate the thinking, not the thought.

words.note: The same qad L3-M7 taught in front of a past, where it means already. In front of a present-shaped verb it means may, and the verb behind it is untouched.

sentences.trap: English needs a modal — may, might, could — and every one of them reshapes the verb after it. Arabic changes nothing: qad is dropped in front and yaʾtī keeps its ordinary present shape.
sentences.sound: qad YAʾ-tī: the hamza inside yaʾtī is a catch in the throat between the two syllables.

variations.cue: The manager may go tomorrow
variations.changed: the verb under qad: coming → going

variations.cue: The idea may be good
variations.changed: a verb of being under qad, and a feminine subject with it

mistake.why: One hedge is enough. L3-M3's rubbamā and qad do the same job, and stacking them is the commonest over-reach once a learner owns both.

sentences.usage: Leaving a plan open without promising anything.
sentences.mnemonic: qad + past = already; qad + present = may.

sentences.display: lasta muwāfiq, wa lā baʾsa fī dhālika
sentences.script: لست موافق، ولا بأس في ذلك
sentences.cue: You don't agree, and there's no harm in that
sentences.literal: Not-you agreeing, and no harm in that

words.note: The rest of L2-M7's laysa: lasta you, lasti you (to a woman), lasnā we, laysū they. lastu, laysa and laysat are already yours.

sentences.trap: English negates with one unchanging word — you are not. Arabic conjugates the negation itself, so the person lives inside laysa rather than beside it.
sentences.sound: LAS-ta: the -ta ending is the same you that sits on dhahabta, here riding the negation instead of a verb.

variations.display: lasti muwāfiqa, wa lā baʾsa fī dhālika
variations.script: لستِ موافقة، ولا بأس في ذلك
variations.cue: You don't agree, and there's no harm in that
variations.changed: who is addressed: a man → a woman, in the negation and in the adjective

variations.cue: We aren't busy today
variations.changed: the person: you → we, and the predicate goes plural with it

mistake.display: anta lā muwāfiq, wa lā baʾsa fī dhālika
mistake.script: أنت لا موافق، ولا بأس في ذلك
mistake.why: lā negates verbs. There is no verb here, so the negation is laysa and its cells, and the person moves inside it.

sentences.usage: Letting somebody off the hook for disagreeing with you.
sentences.mnemonic: The negation takes the person: las- plus the ending you already know.

sentences.cue: It seems the manager is busy today

words.note: A frame, not a verb to conjugate: it stays in the he-form whoever is speaking, and the clause behind ʾanna carries the people.

sentences.trap: English can make this personal — he seems busy. Arabic keeps the frame impersonal and puts everything into the clause behind it: yabdū anna al-mudīr mashghūl.
sentences.sound: YAB-dū AN-na: the long -ū at the end of yabdū never takes a person ending.

variations.cue: It seems the idea is good
variations.changed: the clause behind the frame

variations.cue: It seems the price is high
variations.changed: what is being observed

mistake.why: Without ʾanna the frame has nothing to hold. The clause has to be introduced, and yabdū on its own leaves the sentence in two pieces.

sentences.usage: Reporting an impression you are not prepared to defend.
sentences.mnemonic: yabdū anna — it seems that, always in the he-form.

sentences.display: min al-mumkin an adhhab maʿaka ghadan
sentences.script: من الممكن أن أذهب معكَ غدًا
sentences.cue: It's possible I'll go with you tomorrow
sentences.literal: From the-possible that I-go with-you tomorrow

words.note: Built like L4-M4's min al-wāḍiḥ anna, but ending in an with a present-shaped verb behind it instead of ʾanna with a clause.

sentences.trap: English collapses this into a modal — I might go. Arabic keeps the frame impersonal and the verb ordinary; there is no shape of adhhab that means might go.
sentences.sound: min al-MUM-kin an AD-hab — the an is said so lightly it almost joins the verb behind it.

variations.cue: It's possible I'll go tomorrow
variations.changed: what is dropped: going with you → simply going

variations.cue: It's possible the manager will come
variations.changed: who: I → the manager, in the far verb

mistake.why: an is not optional here. The frame ends in an, and the verb behind it is what an takes; without it there are two halves and no join.

sentences.usage: Half-accepting an invitation, so that a no later costs nothing.
sentences.mnemonic: From the possible THAT I go.

sentences.display: ʿalā ayy ḥāl, sa-attaṣil bika ghadan
sentences.script: على أي حال، سأتصل بك غدًا
sentences.cue: In any case, I'll call you tomorrow
sentences.literal: On any state, will-I-call with-you tomorrow

words.note: L2-M9's ayy inside a frozen phrase, and ayy always takes an indefinite noun. It closes a subject without settling it.

sentences.trap: English anyway can land as dismissal. This phrase does not: it parks the disagreement and moves the conversation on, which is why it belongs in a module about saving face.
sentences.sound: ʿa-lā AYY ḤĀL — three beats, the ayy with a doubled y and the ḥ breathy.

variations.cue: In any case, I'll go tomorrow
variations.changed: what happens next: calling you → going

variations.cue: In any case, I'm not sure
variations.changed: what follows the frame: a plan → a hedge

mistake.display: ʿalā ayy al-ḥāl, sa-attaṣil bika ghadan
mistake.script: على أي الحال، سأتصل بك غدًا
mistake.why: ayy takes an indefinite noun behind it. al-ḥāl with the article breaks a phrase that is frozen as ʿalā ayy ḥāl.

sentences.usage: Ending a disagreement without either side losing.
sentences.mnemonic: Any state at all: ʿalā ayy ḥāl.

sentences.display: ḥasanan, maʿaka ḥaqq, wa lākin lastu muwāfiq
sentences.script: حسنًا، معكَ حق، ولكن لست موافق
sentences.cue: All right, you have a point, but I don't agree
sentences.literal: Well, with-you right, and but not-I agreeing

words.note: The adverbial -an again (L2-M1), on the word for good. It opens a turn and buys a second before the disagreement lands.

sentences.trap: English okay can itself be agreement. ḥasanan is not: it marks only that you heard, which is why the sentence is free to go on and disagree.
sentences.sound: ḤA-sa-nan: the ḥ is the breathy one, and the -an is the ordinary adverbial ending.

variations.display: ḥasanan, maʿaki ḥaqq, wa lākin lastu muwāfiq
variations.script: حسنًا، معكِ حق، ولكن لست موافق
variations.cue: All right, you have a point, but I don't agree
variations.changed: who is answered: a man → a woman

variations.display: ḥasanan, lā aẓunn anna hādhā mumkin
variations.script: حسنًا، لا أظن أن هذا ممكن
variations.cue: All right, I don't think that's possible
variations.changed: the answer: granting a point → doubting it outright

mistake.display: ḥasan, maʿaka ḥaqq, wa lākin lastu muwāfiq
mistake.script: حسن، معكَ حق، ولكن لست موافق
mistake.why: As an opener the word carries the -an. Bare ḥasan is the adjective good, describing a thing, and it cannot open a turn.

sentences.usage: Taking the floor politely when you are about to say no.
sentences.mnemonic: ḥasanan buys a second, not an agreement.

sentences.cue: It's as if he's angry, but I'm not sure

words.note: ka- is a clitic meaning like, written joined the way L1-M2's bi- and L4-M2's fa- are. On L3-M3's annahu it makes as if he.

sentences.trap: English as if is two words and takes anything after it. Arabic's ka- is one letter glued to what follows, and what follows here is ʾanna with its pronoun already attached.
sentences.sound: ka-AN-na-hu: one word, the doubled nn held, and the ka- said so lightly it is easy to miss.

variations.cue: It's as if she's angry, but I'm not sure
variations.changed: the person inside the frame: he → she, and the adjective with it

variations.cue: It's as if he's tired, but I'm not sure
variations.changed: the impression: angry → tired

mistake.display: ka annahu ghāḍib, lākin lastu mutaʾakkidan
mistake.script: ك أنه غاضب، لكن لست متأكداً
mistake.why: ka- is never a word on its own — it is one letter joined to what follows, which is why this course hyphenates it. Standing apart it is not Arabic.

sentences.usage: Describing an impression while flagging that it is only an impression.
sentences.mnemonic: One letter for like, glued on.

sentences.display: hādhā ṣaḥīḥ taqrīban, lākin laysa tamāman
sentences.script: هذا صحيح تقريبًا، لكن ليس تمامًا
sentences.cue: This is almost right, but not completely
sentences.literal: This correct approximately, but not-is completely

words.note: The adverbial -an once more. It sits behind what it softens, in the slot L1-M3's jiddan already taught, and it is the cheapest hedge in the module.

sentences.trap: English almost goes in front of what it softens. Arabic's adverb goes behind it: ṣaḥīḥ taqrīban, the same slot jiddan takes.
sentences.sound: taq-RĪ-ban: the q is the deep k, made at the very back of the throat.

variations.display: hādhā ṣaḥīḥ taqrīban, lākin laysa jayyid
variations.script: هذا صحيح تقريبًا، لكن ليس جيد
variations.cue: This is almost right, but it isn't good
variations.changed: the objection behind the concession

variations.cue: The work is almost good
variations.changed: what is being softened, with the objection dropped

mistake.display: hādhā ṣaḥīḥ taqrīban, lākin lā tamāman
mistake.script: هذا صحيح تقريبًا، لكن لا تمامًا
mistake.why: lā negates a verb and there is no verb here. The negation in a nominal sentence is laysa, exactly as everywhere else in this module.

sentences.usage: Half-agreeing in a way that leaves the door open.
sentences.mnemonic: The softener goes behind, like jiddan.

sentences.display: āsif, lā aẓunn anna hādhā mumkin
sentences.script: آسف، لا أظن أن هذا ممكن
sentences.cue: Sorry, I don't think that's possible
sentences.literal: Sorry, not I-think that this possible

words.note: L3-M3's aẓunn and aʿtaqid under a negative. The negative goes onto the thinking verb, exactly as it does in English — for once the transfer is safe.

sentences.trap: English softens a refusal with a conditional — I wouldn't think so. This ladder has no conditional to soften with: the softening is āsif in front and the negative-raised frame behind it.
sentences.sound: Ā-sif: a long ā at the front, then a short i. The whole line is said slowly — the pause is part of the refusal.

variations.display: āsif, lā aẓunn anna hādhā ṣaḥīḥ
variations.script: آسف، لا أظن أن هذا صحيح
variations.cue: Sorry, I don't think that's right
variations.changed: what is refused: a possibility → a claim

variations.display: āsifa, lā aẓunn anna hādhā mumkin
variations.script: آسفة، لا أظن أن هذا ممكن
variations.cue: Sorry, I don't think that's possible
variations.changed: who is speaking: a man → a woman

mistake.why: It is correct Arabic and the wrong register. The flat negation lands as a ruling; this module's whole point is that the doubt goes on the thinking verb instead.

sentences.usage: Refusing outright, as gently as this level can — the sentence the module was built to reach.
sentences.mnemonic: Sorry first, doubt second, refusal never stated.
